sections.title: From text to model-ready pieces
paragraphs: Imagine a mailroom that cannot route a paragraph as one giant parcel. It first divides the message into labeled pieces, then sends those pieces through the sorting system. A transformer does something similar: it splits text into {{token}}s before the {{model}} can process it.

A {{token}} may be a whole common word, part of a rare word, a number fragment, code punctuation, or whitespace. Tokenization follows a fixed vocabulary, so 100 words do not reliably equal 100 {{token}}s. Technical text, unusual names, and some languages often use more pieces than plain English prose.

Each {{token}} ID is mapped to an {{embedding}}, a list of numbers the {{model}} can calculate with. The transformer also needs information about position, because the same pieces in "model scores answer" and "answer scores model" should not mean the same thing. Layers repeatedly update these representations using surrounding context.

The {{contextWindow}} is the amount of tokenized material available for one request. It must hold the instructions, examples, retrieved context, user input, and often room for the answer. If an AiEval judge prompt spends most of that budget repeating source material, the rubric or response may be truncated or crowded out.

Token counts therefore connect architecture to practical decisions: request limits, output caps, latency, and provider cost. Counting words is only an estimate; production code should use provider usage data or the matching tokenizer when the exact budget matters.
bullets: Position changes meaning, so order must be represented as well as content.
The {{contextWindow}} budget includes more than the visible user question.

check.prompt: An AiEval judge request fits under a provider's 8,000-word estimate but is rejected for exceeding its 8,000-{{token}} {{contextWindow}}. Which diagnosis is most useful?
check.answer: Words and tokens are not one-to-one, so measure the actual tokenized request
choices: The provider counted randomly, so retry the identical request
Words and tokens are not one-to-one, so measure the actual tokenized request
Only generated answers count toward the context window
Convert every space to a newline because newlines use no tokens
check.explanation: A word can become one or several {{token}}s, and punctuation or code can add more. The complete request—not just the user-visible question—uses the {{contextWindow}}, so inspect actual usage and shorten low-value context.

sections.title: Attention builds context
paragraphs: After the mailroom labels each piece, the sorter must decide which earlier pieces help interpret the current one. {{attention}} performs that routing: for each position, it computes how strongly information from other allowed positions should influence the next representation.

Transformers do this through several attention heads in each layer. One head may connect a pronoun to a name, another may track an output-format instruction, and another may relate a claim to supporting evidence. Their results are combined and transformed again, so context becomes richer over many layers.

For text generation, a position normally attends only to available earlier {{token}}s, not future text that has not been generated. The learned {{weights}} determine how those comparisons work; the specific {{prompt}} determines which relationships become useful on this request. That is why changing one instruction can shift the continuation.

Consider an AiEval {{judge}} reading a {{rubric}}, a candidate answer, and source evidence. To produce a score, it needs to connect claims in the answer with the relevant {{criterion}} and evidence. Clear labels and focused context make those relationships easier to use than a long prompt full of repeated boilerplate.

{{attention}} is not a truth detector or a guaranteed explanation of the {{model}}'s reasoning. A transformer can emphasize relevant text and still make a bad {{prediction}}, miss a detail in a long context, or follow a misleading instruction. You still need test cases and evaluation rather than assuming that available context was used correctly.

reveals.prompt: A judge must score factual accuracy. What relationships need to be available?
reveals.reveal: Claims in the candidate answer need to connect with the provided evidence and the factual-accuracy {{criterion}}. Merely placing all three in the {{prompt}} does not guarantee a correct score.

reveals.prompt: Two answers are identical except one includes a required citation. What relationship matters?
reveals.reveal: The citation-format instruction must connect with the citation text in the answer. A well-anchored {{rubric}} makes that requirement explicit for the {{judge}}.

reveals.prompt: A long transcript contains ten repeated greetings before the actual request. What is the practical risk?
reveals.reveal: The greetings consume {{token}} budget and add irrelevant context. The request remains available, but long noisy prompts can make reliable use of the important instruction harder.

check.prompt: An AiEval {{judge}} often misses a short {{rubric}} placed after a huge duplicated transcript. Which change best applies what you learned?
check.answer: Remove duplicated context, label the rubric clearly, and re-evaluate the judge
choices: Add more copies of the transcript so every detail appears repeatedly
Remove duplicated context, label the rubric clearly, and re-evaluate the judge
Assume attention always finds the rubric and ignore the failures
Replace rubric criteria with a vague request to score fairly
check.explanation: Focused context and explicit structure make the relationship between the answer and each {{criterion}} easier for the {{model}} to use. Re-running the {{evaluation}} is essential because {{attention}} improves contextual routing but does not guarantee correct judging.

sections.title: Apply transformers in AiEval
paragraphs: A generative transformer is trained by repeatedly predicting a missing next {{token}} from earlier context. Its guess is compared with the actual next {{target}}, {{loss}} measures the error, and training adjusts the {{weights}}. Across enormous text collections, this simple objective teaches reusable language and task patterns—but not a database of guaranteed facts.

At runtime, the {{model}} repeats one loop: read the current context, produce probabilities for the next {{token}}, choose one, append it, and continue. Your {{prompt}}, examples, {{temperature}}, and output limit shape that loop. The result can be useful and coherent while still being an unsupported continuation.

Apply this in AiEval by comparing models on a concrete support task. Keep the user request, evidence, output constraints, and {{rubric}} consistent; then inspect whether each answer follows the instruction, uses the evidence, and stays within the requested format. Variation in wording is expected, so score behavior rather than demanding one exact sentence.

Architecture-aware debugging gives you better hypotheses. A cut-off JSON answer may point to an output-{{token}} cap; a missed rule may point to crowded context or unclear structure; a confident unsupported claim shows that likely next text is not the same as verified truth. Change one condition, rerun the {{evaluation}}, and use results instead of guessing at hidden internals.

The optional **Transformers lab** lets you adjust a tiny teaching example and watch attention and next-token preference change. Its hand-set visualization is a shortcut, not a faithful view inside a production {{largeLanguageModel}}. Continue next to **Production concerns**, where this token-by-token process becomes a system problem involving cost, latency, reliability, and safety.
bullets: Hold task and {{rubric}} constant when comparing {{model}}s.
Treat token limits and prompt structure as testable failure hypotheses.
Measure instruction-following and evidence use, not exact wording alone.

check.prompt: A {{judge}} gives more influence to "must cite evidence" than to a greeting while producing score JSON. In one short phrase, what is {{attention}} doing?
check.answer: Weighing which prior tokens are most relevant
check.explanation: {{attention}} routes more influence from context that is useful for the current {{prediction}}. Here the citation constraint is more relevant to scoring and formatting than the greeting, although the final score still needs evaluation.

recapQuestions.prompt: A model comparison includes a long document, two candidate answers, and a rubric. The judge output is repeatedly cut off before valid JSON closes. What should you test first?
recapQuestions.answer: Shorten low-value input context and reserve enough output tokens
choices: Increase temperature so the closing brace appears by chance
Shorten low-value input context and reserve enough output tokens
Duplicate both answers to strengthen attention
Remove the rubric because judging does not need criteria
recapQuestions.explanation: The request and generated answer compete within practical token limits, while a separate output cap may stop generation early. Reduce irrelevant input, set a sufficient output allowance, and rerun the same {{testCase}} before blaming model quality.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why should AiEval score a transformer's answer against evidence and a {{rubric}} instead of trusting fluent wording?
recapQuestions.answer: Next-token prediction can produce plausible but unsupported text
choices: Next-token prediction can produce plausible but unsupported text
Attention prevents the model from reading any evidence
Tokenization removes all factual information from prompts
A fluent answer is always copied exactly from training data
recapQuestions.explanation: A transformer is optimized to continue context with likely {{token}}s, not to guarantee truth. Evidence-based criteria let an {{evaluation}} distinguish a grounded answer from a convincing {{hallucination}}.
